title: Multiplication Table Printer
story: Your younger cousin is learning multiplication tables, staring at a boring worksheet. You decide to build a function that prints any times table on demand — from 1×7 to 10×7 — making math practice feel like a magic trick.
why: A void function containing a while loop and formatted output teaches the pattern of generating structured, repeated output — a foundation for reports, tables, and data displays.
analogy: A void function like `print_table` is like a microwave — you press a button, it does work (heats food), but you don't 'get' anything back except the completed action. A value-returning function like `sum_to` is like a vending machine — you put in money, and you receive a product (the return value) in exchange.
try_it: Extend `print_table` to accept a second parameter `up_to: Int` so the table prints from 1×n to up_to×n instead of always stopping at 10. Then write a `print_all_tables(max: Int)` function that prints tables 1 through max using a loop.
tips: A void function has no `-> ReturnType` — it does work but produces no value
The loop inside print_table runs exactly 10 times, from i=1 to i=10
Use clear labels like 'Table of 7:' before calling print_table for readability
You can call the same void function multiple times with different arguments
common_mistakes: Adding `-> Int` or `-> Str` to print_table — it doesn't return anything
Starting i at 0 instead of 1 — multiplication tables start at 1×n
Using `< 10` instead of `<= 10` — only prints 9 lines instead of 10
Trying to capture the result with `let x = print_table(5)` — void functions can't be captured
